cards.text: Isaiah son of Amoz saw this vision about Judah and Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:1). God has just told His people to wash themselves clean and stop doing evil (Isaiah 1:16). Now Isaiah says, "See how the faithful city has become a harlot!"

cards.question: Isaiah says the city was once full of justice, with righteousness living inside her. Who does he say is in her now?

cards.text: Then Isaiah says, "Your silver has become dross." That's like opening a cookie box you KNOW was full and finding crumbs. Just crumbs. Staring back at you.

cards.question: Isaiah says the city's fine wine is now diluted with ___.

cards.text: Then Isaiah says the city's rulers are rebels and friends of thieves. Friends of THIEVES, baker. That's not a résumé line, that's a warning label.

cards.question: Isaiah says the rulers of the city all love something. What is it?
Back in Isaiah 1:17, God told His people to defend the fatherless. True or false: the city's rulers defend the fatherless.

cards.text: Then comes "Therefore," and the Lord GOD of Hosts, the Mighty One of Israel, declares what He will do. Friend, whenever I hear "therefore," I sit up a little straighter on my gold base.

cards.question: The Lord GOD of Hosts says He will be relieved of His foes. What does He say He'll do to His enemies?

cards.text: Then the Lord says, "I will turn My hand against you." If I heard that, I'd dive face-first into the chocolate chips, gold base and all. But keep listening.

cards.question: The Lord says He will thoroughly purge something from the city and remove all its impurities. What will He purge?
After the purge, the Lord says He will restore the city's judges as at first and its counselors as at the beginning.
After that, the Lord says the city will be called the City of ___, the ___ City.

cards.text: Here's where my mustache starts waving. Zion, another name for Jerusalem, the same city whose silver turned to dross, "will be redeemed with justice".

cards.question: Isaiah says some of Zion's people will be redeemed with righteousness. Who are they?
Isaiah says rebels and those who forsake the LORD will be redeemed right along with Zion's repentant ones.

cards.text: Then Isaiah says the people will be ashamed of the sacred oaks they delighted in, and embarrassed by the gardens they chose. Kind of like me back in the day, stamping blurry cookies and calling it "my new style."

cards.question: Isaiah says the people will become like an oak whose leaves are ___, like a garden without water.

cards.text: Last picture. The strong man becomes tinder, his work becomes a spark, and both burn together.

cards.question: When the strong man and his work burn together, someone will be there to put out the flames.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The card spends words explaining a hard word ("Zion, another name for Jerusalem"). The dictionary pop-up should cover Zion instead.

rule.text: Don't spend card words explaining a hard word. Hard words get a dictionary pop-up (definitions.md, made after the cards).

findings.problem: Isaiah 1:28 is only tested as a false statement. No card ever says what actually happens: rebels and sinners will be shattered together, and those who forsake the LORD will perish. The baker leaves without this key turn in the passage. Add a story card that tells it.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The text says "you will be ashamed" right after 1:28 names the rebels, sinners and those who forsake the LORD. The card calls the "you" "the people," which decides who is spoken to. It also seems to include the repentant ones redeemed in 1:27.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The question says "the people will become like an oak." Isaiah 1:30 says "you," so the card decides who is spoken to.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The verse is about being ashamed of what you delighted in and chose. The joke is about calling blurry cookies "my new style," which is about spinning a flaw. The shame never shows up, so the comparison doesn't share the verse's action.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The joke adds a new moment to his backstory in the Millers' kitchen: he called his worn-out stamps "my new style." Jokes may invent small moments around his bakery, not new details in his backstory.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.
